subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Affect Heuristic: Feeling Is Believing
description: A 60-second lesson on Affect Heuristic: Feeling Is Believing.

hook.text: People told nuclear power is 'clean' rate its risks lower. Same technology, different framing, different fear.

buildup.text: Slovic found that our emotional reaction to a topic shapes our beliefs about its risks and benefits.

discovery.text: Affect heuristic: we use current feelings as data. If it feels good, it seems safe. If scary, it seems dangerous.

twist.text: Good mood makes you rate unrelated investments as safer. Your emotional weather colors all judgments.

climax.text: Feelings arrive before analysis. By the time you think, emotion has already voted on the answer.

punchline.text: You feel the answer before you think it.

quiz.question: What does the affect heuristic use as data?

details.summary: The affect heuristic replaces complex analysis with emotional gut reactions. If something feels good, people judge it as low-risk and high-benefit; if it feels bad, they see it as high-risk and low-benefit. Feelings become the proxy for facts.
details.whyItMatters: Emotional reactions to technologies, investments, and policies shape public risk perception more than data does. Understanding the affect heuristic explains why some objectively safe technologies are feared while riskier familiar ones are accepted.
takeaways: Positive feelings reduce perceived risk and boost perceived benefit simultaneously
Negative emotional associations inflate risk perception regardless of data
Time pressure strengthens reliance on the affect heuristic over analysis

faq.question: How does the affect heuristic reverse the relationship between risk and benefit?
faq.answer: In reality, higher benefits often come with higher risks. But the affect heuristic creates an inverse perception: liked activities seem both safe and beneficial, while disliked activities seem both dangerous and useless, contradicting objective evidence.

faq.question: When is the affect heuristic actually helpful?
faq.answer: For experienced professionals in familiar domains, emotional responses encode accumulated expertise. A veteran firefighter's gut feeling about a dangerous structure is the affect heuristic powered by pattern recognition. The trap is applying it to novel or complex situations.
